objectives.label: Parts and equality of complex numbers
objectives.description: Identify the real and imaginary parts of a complex number a + bi (including real numbers and numbers such as 2i) and use equality of complex numbers to find real x and y.

objectives.label: Add, subtract, multiply complex numbers
objectives.description: Calculate sums, differences, products and powers of complex numbers, substituting i² = −1, and give the answer in the form a + bi.

objectives.label: Conjugates and dividing complex numbers
objectives.description: State the complex conjugate of a complex number and divide complex numbers by multiplying numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the denominator, answering in the form a + bi.

objectives.label: Square roots of negative numbers
objectives.description: Express square roots of negative numbers in terms of i and calculate with them.

entries.text: Picture of a technician at an MRI/ECG machine with a screen titled 'Biological Signals: Waves & Complex Numbers', showing a complex-plane diagram with small labels (amplitude, phase, etc.); text too small to read reliably.

A.why: Decorative opening picture about biological signals, not teaching a specific objective.

B.why: Decorative real-world picture introducing the lesson.

entries.text: The number whose square is −1 is denoted by i; that is, i² = −1. $i^2=-1$

A.why: Defines i with i² = −1, the basis for parts of a + bi, used first in identifying parts.

B.why: Introduces i with i² = −1, which underlies the whole lesson.

entries.text: A number expressed in the form a + bi using two real numbers a, b is called a complex number. $a+bi$

A.why: Defines the complex number a + bi whose real and imaginary parts are identified.

B.why: Defines a complex number a + bi, whose parts are then identified.

entries.text: When b = 0, a + bi becomes a real number. $b=0$

A.why: When b = 0 the number is real, part of classifying real/imaginary parts.

B.why: When b = 0 the number is real, a case of identifying the parts.

entries.text: When b ≠ 0, a + bi is called an imaginary number. $b\neq 0$

A.why: When b ≠ 0 it is an imaginary number, classifying by the imaginary part.

B.why: Defines an imaginary number as a + bi with b ≠ 0, classifying by parts.

entries.text: When a, b are real numbers, if a + bi = 0, then a = 0, b = 0. $a=0,\ b=0$

A.why: If a + bi = 0 then a = 0 and b = 0, used for equality of complex numbers.

B.why: Equality rule: a + bi = 0 means a = 0 and b = 0.

entries.text: Side diagram: 'Complex Numbers' band split into 'Imaginary Numbers' (−2i, 8i) in blue and 'Real Numbers' (7, −√3) in pink. Note: 'Real numbers are also part of Complex numbers.'

A.why: Diagram showing real and imaginary numbers as kinds of complex numbers, like 2i and 7.

B.why: Shows imaginary and real numbers as parts of complex numbers.

entries.text: Powers of i should be calculated by expressing them in terms of i². Example: i⁸ = (i²)⁴ = (−1)⁴ = 1; i⁷ = i × (i²)³ = i × (−1)³ = −i. $i^8=(i^2)^4=(-1)^4=1,\ i^7=i\times(i^2)^3=i\times(-1)^3=-i$

A.why: Powers of i are calculated using i² = −1 in computations.

B.why: Powers of i are calculated through i² = −1.

entries.text: Misconceptions: Mixing real and imaginary parts: adding or subtracting unlike terms together instead of keeping real and imaginary parts separate. Errors in multiplication: when expanding brackets, forgetting that i × i = i² = −1.

A.why: Warns about errors when adding and multiplying complex numbers, such as forgetting i² = −1.

B.why: Warns about errors in adding and multiplying complex numbers, such as forgetting i² = −1.

entries.text: The product of conjugate complex numbers is a real number.

A.why: The product of conjugates is a real number, used in division.

B.why: Product of conjugates is real, the fact behind conjugate division.

entries.text: For fractional expressions containing imaginary numbers in the denominator, first multiply both numerator and denominator by the complex conjugate of the denominator to make the denominator a real number.

A.why: Divide by multiplying numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the denominator.

B.why: Dividing by multiplying top and bottom by the denominator's conjugate.

entries.text: When the inside of the square root is a negative number, calculate after expressing it in a form in terms of i.

A.why: Write the square root of a negative number using i before calculating.

B.why: Method for calculating with square roots of negatives by writing them with i.

entries.text: Misconception: thinking √−n is undefined or impossible. Students may believe negative numbers cannot have square roots at all, rather than understanding that complex numbers extend the system to make this possible.

A.why: Corrects the belief that square roots of negative numbers do not exist.

B.why: Addresses the belief that negative numbers have no square root.

entries.text: Misconception: confusing signs. Some assume √−n = −√n, which is incorrect; the correct form is √−n = i√n. $\sqrt{-n}=i\sqrt{n}$

A.why: Corrects the sign error: √−n = i√n, not −√n.

B.why: Warns that √−n = i√n, not −√n, about square roots of negatives.

objectives.label: Solve quadratic equations
objectives.description: Solve quadratic equations in the set of complex numbers, using square roots, factorisation or the quadratic formula, expressing negative square roots in terms of i.

objectives.label: Use the discriminant
objectives.description: Determine the nature of the solutions of a quadratic equation using the discriminant, and find the range of a constant for which the solutions are real, repeated or imaginary.

objectives.label: Roots and coefficients
objectives.description: Calculate sums, products and expressions in the roots of a quadratic equation, and find constants from a stated relationship between the two solutions.

objectives.label: Factorise over complex numbers
objectives.description: Factorise quadratic expressions, including quartics in x², over the set of complex numbers as a(x − α)(x − β) using the solutions of the equation.

objectives.label: Form equations; signs of roots
objectives.description: Form a quadratic equation from given roots or from expressions in the roots of another equation, find two numbers from their sum and product, and determine the range of a constant from the signs of the two solutions using D, α+β and αβ.

entries.text: Diagram of reproductive rate (vertical axis) against Generation/Time (horizontal axis) with a parabola-like curve, DNA helix, labels 'Stable Population', 'Stable Zone', 'Replacement Rate', 'Extinction Event', 'Negative Feedback', 'Adaptive Radiation', 'Collapse/Extinction', 'Gene Diversity'. Text too small to read fully; verify.

A.why: Opening population-biology diagram motivates the lesson but teaches no objective.

B.why: Decorative lesson-opening illustration of a population model.

entries.text: When the inside of the square root is negative, express it in a form in terms of i.

A.why: Tells how to write negative square roots using i when solving.

B.why: Express negative square roots in terms of i when solving.

entries.text: Solve using square roots: the solutions of $x^2=a$ are $x=\pm\sqrt{a}$. $x^2=a \Rightarrow x=\pm\sqrt{a}$

A.why: Solving x²=a by square roots.

B.why: Solving using square roots of x²=a.

entries.text: For $(x+m)^2=a$, transform to $x+m=\pm\sqrt{a}$, so $x=-m\pm\sqrt{a}$. $(x+m)^2=a \Rightarrow x=-m\pm\sqrt{a}$

A.why: Solving (x+m)²=a by square roots.

B.why: Solving using square roots of (x+m)²=a.

entries.text: Solve using factorisation: the solutions of $x(x-a)=0$ are $x=0$ or $a$. $x(x-a)=0 \Rightarrow x=0 \text{ or } a$

A.why: Solving by factorisation, x(x−a)=0.

B.why: Solving by factorisation x(x−a)=0.

entries.text: The solutions of $(x-a)(x-b)=0$ are $x=a$ or $b$. $(x-a)(x-b)=0 \Rightarrow x=a \text{ or } b$

A.why: Solving by factorisation, (x−a)(x−b)=0.

B.why: Solving by factorisation (x−a)(x−b)=0.

entries.text: The solution of $(x-a)^2=0$ is $x=a$. $(x-a)^2=0 \Rightarrow x=a$

A.why: Solving by factorisation, (x−a)²=0.

B.why: Solving by factorisation with a perfect square.

entries.text: The solutions of $(ax-b)(cx-d)=0$ are $x=\frac{b}{a}$ or $\frac{d}{c}$. $(ax-b)(cx-d)=0 \Rightarrow x=\frac{b}{a} \text{ or } \frac{d}{c}$

A.why: Solving by factorisation, (ax−b)(cx−d)=0.

B.why: Solving by factorisation with (ax−b)(cx−d)=0.

entries.text: Solve using the quadratic formula: the solutions of $ax^2+bx+c=0$ are $x=\frac{-b\pm\sqrt{b^2-4ac}}{2a}$. $x=\frac{-b\pm\sqrt{b^2-4ac}}{2a}$

A.why: The quadratic formula for solving equations.

B.why: Solving with the quadratic formula.

entries.text: When D > 0, the equation has two distinct real solutions. $D>0$

A.why: D>0 gives two distinct real solutions.

B.why: D>0 means two distinct real solutions.

entries.text: When D = 0, the equation has a repeated solution (one real solution). $D=0$

A.why: D=0 gives a repeated solution.

B.why: D=0 means a repeated solution.

entries.text: When D < 0, the equation has two distinct imaginary solutions. $D<0$

A.why: D<0 gives two imaginary solutions.

B.why: D<0 means two imaginary solutions.

entries.text: When D ≥ 0 (the cases D > 0 and D = 0, bracketed together), the equation has real solutions. $D\ge 0$

A.why: D≥0 gives real solutions, used for ranges of a constant.

B.why: D≥0 means real solutions.

entries.text: Misconception: with D < 0, thinking there are "no solutions at all", while the correct answer is two complex solutions.

A.why: Misconception about the nature of solutions when D<0.

B.why: Misconception about D<0 giving two complex solutions.

entries.text: Misconception: with D = 0, thinking there are "no solutions", while the correct answer is one repeated real solution.

A.why: Misconception about the nature of solutions when D=0.

B.why: Misconception about D=0 giving a repeated solution.

entries.text: Misconception: with D > 0, thinking there is "only one solution", while the correct answer is two distinct real solutions.

A.why: Misconception about the nature of solutions when D>0.

B.why: Misconception about D>0 giving two distinct real solutions.

entries.text: Upward parabola crossing the m-axis at m = −2 and m = 6, with the part of the axis between −2 and 6 highlighted in red (where the parabola is below the axis). Axis labelled m.

A.why: Parabola in m shows the range of m from a discriminant inequality.

B.why: Parabola in m showing range of m where discriminant is negative or positive.

entries.text: Upward parabola crossing the k-axis at k = −6 and k = 2. Axis labelled k.

A.why: Parabola in k shows the range of k from a discriminant inequality.

B.why: Parabola in k showing range of constant from discriminant inequality.

entries.text: Misconception - Confusing sum and product: some students swap them, thinking the product is $-b/a$ and the sum is $c/a$. $-b/a$, $c/a$

A.why: Warns about swapping sum −b/a and product c/a of roots.

B.why: Warns against swapping sum −b/a and product c/a.

entries.text: Misconception - Ignoring the coefficient a: students sometimes assume formulas are just $-b$ and $c$, forgetting to divide by $a$.

A.why: Warns not to forget dividing by a in sum and product.

B.why: Misconception about forgetting to divide by a in sum and product.

entries.text: The product of the roots is c over a. $\alpha\beta=\frac{c}{a}$

A.why: Product of the roots is c/a.

B.why: Product of roots is c/a.

entries.text: For values of expressions involving solutions of quadratic equations, first find the values of $\alpha+\beta$ and $\alpha\beta$. Rewrite the given expression in terms of $\alpha+\beta$ and $\alpha\beta$, and solve using the relationship between roots and coefficients.

A.why: Evaluating expressions in the roots via α+β and αβ.

B.why: Evaluating expressions in the roots using sum and product.

entries.text: Often-used transformation: sum of squares of the roots. $\alpha^2+\beta^2=(\alpha+\beta)^2-2\alpha\beta$

A.why: α²+β² in terms of sum and product.

B.why: Sum of squares of roots in terms of α+β and αβ.

entries.text: Often-used transformation: sum of cubes of the roots. $\alpha^3+\beta^3=(\alpha+\beta)^3-3\alpha\beta(\alpha+\beta)$

A.why: α³+β³ in terms of sum and product.

B.why: Sum of cubes of roots in terms of α+β and αβ.

entries.text: For problems where the relationship between two solutions is known, let α be one solution, and for the other, express it in terms of α.

A.why: Finding constants from a stated relationship between the two roots.

B.why: Finding constants from a stated relationship between two roots.

entries.text: Be careful not to forget the coefficient a of x².

A.why: Reminder about the coefficient a when factorising a(x−α)(x−β).

B.why: Do not forget coefficient a in a(x−α)(x−β).

entries.text: Misconceptions: Forgetting the coefficient of x². Students often try to split the middle term without considering the leading coefficient a.

A.why: Misconception about forgetting the leading coefficient when factorising.

B.why: Forgetting the leading coefficient when factorising.

entries.text: Misconceptions: Assuming all quadratics factorise neatly. Some believe every quadratic can be factorised into integers, ignoring cases where the discriminant is not a perfect square.

A.why: Misconception that every quadratic factorises neatly into integers, so complex factorisation is needed.

B.why: Misconception about quadratics not factorising neatly, relevant to factorising over complex numbers.

entries.text: Be careful not to forget the coefficient 2 of x².

A.why: Reminder of the coefficient 2 of x² when factorising.

B.why: Reminder about coefficient 2 of x² when factorising as a(x−α)(x−β).

entries.text: Upward-opening parabola on x and y axes, vertex below the x-axis, crossing the x-axis at two orange points labelled α (left of the y-axis) and β (right of the y-axis). Positions read from the figure.

A.why: Parabola with roots α<0<β illustrates the signs of the roots.

B.why: Parabola with roots on either side of the y-axis illustrates roots of different signs.

entries.text: For problems where the signs of the two solutions of a quadratic equation are known, form and solve simultaneous inequalities based on the conditions.

A.why: Uses inequalities from the signs of the roots to find a constant's range.

B.why: Method for sign-of-roots problems using simultaneous inequalities.

entries.text: (i) Two distinct positive solutions imply D > 0, α+β > 0, αβ > 0. $D>0,\ \alpha+\beta>0,\ \alpha\beta>0$

A.why: Conditions for two distinct positive roots.

B.why: Two positive roots conditions on D, α+β, αβ.

entries.text: (ii) Two distinct negative solutions imply D > 0, α+β < 0, αβ > 0. $D>0,\ \alpha+\beta<0,\ \alpha\beta>0$

A.why: Conditions for two distinct negative roots.

B.why: Two negative roots conditions on D, α+β, αβ.

entries.text: (iii) Solutions with different signs imply αβ < 0. $\alpha\beta<0$

A.why: Roots of different signs imply αβ<0.

B.why: Roots of different signs give αβ<0, a sign-of-roots condition.

entries.text: Common Mistakes: writing α+β < 0, −2m < 0, therefore m > 0 is wrong; you forgot the negative sign in the formula.

A.why: Common sign mistake when using α+β in the sign conditions.

B.why: Warns about sign error in α+β when using sign conditions on roots.

entries.text: Number line for m with marked points −6, −2, 0, 3 (open circles). Lines for conditions (i) (m<−2 or m>3), (ii) (m<0), (iii) (m>−6) are drawn at different heights; the common overlap between −6 and −2 is shaded pink/hatched.

A.why: Number line combines the sign conditions to give the range of m.

B.why: Number line combining conditions on m from D, α+β, αβ for positive/negative roots.

objectives.label: Remainder Theorem, linear divisors
objectives.description: Use the Remainder Theorem to find the remainder when a polynomial is divided by a linear expression x − a or ax − b, by evaluating P(a) or P(b/a), and find an unknown coefficient or make a divisibility condition hold.

objectives.label: Remainder for quadratic divisors
objectives.description: Determine the remainder ax + b when a polynomial is divided by a quadratic expression, by writing P(x) = (x − α)(x − β)Q(x) + ax + b, substituting the roots and solving simultaneous equations.

objectives.label: Synthetic division
objectives.description: Use synthetic division to find the quotient and remainder when a polynomial is divided by x − a, inserting a zero coefficient for missing terms.

objectives.label: Factorise using Factor Theorem
objectives.description: Factorise polynomials using the Factor Theorem, finding a value a with P(a) = 0 from the divisors of the constant term, then dividing out the factor x − a.

entries.text: Picture of a woman presenting in front of screens with charts, titled 'Polynomial Theorems for Economic Trends'. Illustrative; carries no maths values.

A.why: Decorative lesson-opening picture with no maths values.

B.why: Decorative lesson-opening picture with no maths.

entries.text: The remainder when P(x) is divided by the linear expression ax − b is P(b/a). $P\left(\frac{b}{a}\right)$

A.why: States the Remainder Theorem for divisor ax − b, giving P(b/a).

B.why: Remainder on division by ax − b is P(b/a).

entries.text: Divisor confusion: students may substitute the wrong value (e.g., use x = 2 instead of x = 2/3 for 3x − 2). $x=2$ instead of $x=\frac{2}{3}$ for $3x-2$

A.why: Warns about substituting x = 2 instead of 2/3 for 3x − 2 in the Remainder Theorem.

B.why: Warns about the wrong substitution value for 3x − 2 in the Remainder Theorem.

entries.text: Picture in Challenge box: a researcher pointing at a whiteboard titled 'Income distribution model I(x)' showing 2x^3−3x^2+ax+6 with an arrow to (2x+1) (divisor), 'x = YEARS since new economic policy', 'Validity & stability condition'. Whiteboard text read from image; verify.

A.why: Challenge on finding the unknown a in a cubic divided by 2x+1 for a validity condition.

B.why: Challenge picture about finding a so that divisor 2x+1 works, a Remainder Theorem condition.

entries.text: If P(x) is divided by a quadratic expression (x − α)(x − β), let the quotient be Q(x) and the remainder be ax + b. (Side note: the degree of the remainder must be lower than the degree of the divisor.) $(x-\alpha)(x-\beta)$

A.why: Sets quotient Q(x) and remainder ax + b for a quadratic divisor.

B.why: Sets quotient Q(x) and remainder ax + b for a quadratic divisor.

entries.text: (x − α)(x − β)Q(x) becomes 0 when x = α or x = β is substituted. $(x-\alpha)(x-\beta)Q(x)=0$

A.why: Substituting α or β makes the product term zero, used to find the remainder.

B.why: The quotient term vanishes when x = α or β, giving equations.

entries.text: If P(x) is divided by a quadratic expression (x − α)(x − β), the remainder is of the form ax + b. $(x-\alpha)(x-\beta)$

A.why: Remainder on division by a quadratic has the form ax + b.

B.why: Remainder on a quadratic divisor has the form ax + b.

entries.text: Let the quotient be Q(x) and the remainder be ax + b. $Q(x),\ ax+b$

A.why: Names the quotient Q(x) and remainder ax + b for quadratic division.

B.why: Names quotient Q(x) and remainder ax + b for a quadratic divisor.

entries.text: Express it as P(x) = (x − α)(x − β)Q(x) + ax + b. $P(x)=(x-\alpha)(x-\beta)Q(x)+ax+b$

A.why: Writes P(x) = (x − α)(x − β)Q(x) + ax + b.

B.why: States P(x)=(x−α)(x−β)Q(x)+ax+b.

entries.text: The degree of the remainder must be lower than the degree of the divisor.

A.why: Remainder degree must be below the quadratic divisor's, so it is ax + b.

B.why: Remainder degree must be lower than the quadratic divisor, so it is ax + b.

entries.text: Misconception: forgetting to insert a zero coefficient for missing terms (like the $x^2$ term).

A.why: Synthetic division needs a zero coefficient for missing terms.

B.why: Warns to insert zero coefficients for missing terms in synthetic division.

entries.text: Misconception: mixing up the quotient coefficients with the remainder.

A.why: Warns against mixing quotient coefficients with the remainder in synthetic division.

B.why: Misconception about quotient coefficients versus remainder in synthetic division.

entries.text: Step 1: Extract the coefficients of $x^3+5x+11$: 1, 0, 5, 11. Side note: since there is no $x^2$ term, the coefficient is 0. $x^3+5x+11$

A.why: Step 1 of synthetic division: extract coefficients, with 0 for the missing x² term.

B.why: Step 1 of synthetic division: extract coefficients, with 0 for missing term.

entries.text: Step 2: Since dividing by $x+2$, write $-2$ on the left, before the row 1, 0, 5, 11. Side note: when dividing by $x-a$, write the value of $a$ on the left.

A.why: Step 2 of synthetic division: write a on the left.

B.why: Step 2 of synthetic division: write a on the left.

entries.text: Step 3: Bring down the first number 1 as is, multiply by $-2$ written on the left, and write the answer in the second row.

A.why: Step 3 of synthetic division: bring down 1 and multiply by the divisor value.

B.why: Step 3 of synthetic division.

entries.text: Synthetic division layout with -2 on the left; top row 1, 0, 5, 11; arrow brings 1 down to the third row; pink arrow from 1 to -2 written in the second row under 0; line under second row.

A.why: Shows the synthetic division layout for steps 1–3.

B.why: Synthetic division layout showing bringing down and multiplying.

entries.text: Step 4: Add the two numbers vertically.

A.why: Step 4 of synthetic division: add vertically.

B.why: Step 4 of synthetic division: add vertically.

entries.text: Layout: -2 | 1 0 5 11; second row: -2 (under 0); third row: 1, -2.

A.why: Shows the synthetic division table after the addition step.

B.why: Layout of the synthetic division in progress.

entries.text: Step 5: Repeat steps 3 and 4 until the right end of the 3rd row is filled. Side note: from right to left: Remainder, Constant term of Quotient, Coefficient of x, Coefficient of $x^2$, ..., Coefficient of $x^n$.

A.why: Step 5 of synthetic division: repeat and read off quotient and remainder.

B.why: Step 5 of the synthetic division procedure.

entries.text: Completed table: -2 | 1 0 5 11; second row: -2, 4, -18; third row: 1, -2, 9, -7 with -7 boxed (the remainder).

A.why: Completed synthetic division table with remainder −7.

B.why: Completed synthetic division table giving remainder −7.

entries.text: If a polynomial P(x) is divisible by the linear expression x − a, it can be factorised as P(x) = (x − a)Q(x). $P(x)=(x-a)Q(x)$

A.why: If P(x) is divisible by x − a, it factorises as (x − a)Q(x).

B.why: Factor form P(x)=(x−a)Q(x) used in factorising.

entries.text: Values for a are easy to find by substituting ±(divisors of the constant term) in order.

A.why: Find a by trying ± divisors of the constant term.

B.why: Tells how to find a with P(a)=0 from divisors of the constant term.

entries.text: Synthetic division by 1: top row 1, 2, −1, −2; middle row 1, 3, 2; bottom row 1, 3, 2, 0 (remainder 0 boxed). Divisor 1 boxed at left.

A.why: Synthetic division by 1 with remainder 0 to factorise the cubic.

B.why: Synthetic division by 1 used to divide out the factor after finding P(1)=0 in factorisation.

entries.text: Synthetic division of $x^4-6x^3+8x^2+8x-16$ by $x-2$: divisor 2; coefficients 1, −6, 8, 8, −16; second row 2, −8, 0, 16; bottom row 1, −4, 0, 8, remainder 0.

A.why: Synthetic division by x − 2 with remainder 0 to factorise the quartic.

B.why: Synthetic division of a quartic by x − 2.

entries.text: Synthetic division of $x^3-4x^2+8$ by $x-2$: divisor 2; coefficients 1, −4, 0, 8; second row 2, −4, −8; bottom row 1, −2, −4, remainder 0.

A.why: Synthetic division by x − 2 with remainder 0 to factorise the cubic.

B.why: Synthetic division example with a zero inserted for the missing x term.

objectives.label: Solve higher-degree equations
objectives.description: Solve cubic and quartic equations by factorising (sum of cubes, the Factor Theorem, or treating x^2 as a chunk), using the Quadratic Formula for non-factorisable parts, and find all real and complex solutions.

objectives.label: Determine cubic coefficients
objectives.description: Determine unknown coefficients of a cubic equation from given solutions (including complex ones) by substitution, and find the other solutions.

objectives.label: Simplify expressions with ω
objectives.description: Simplify and evaluate expressions involving the cube root of unity ω using ω^3=1 and ω^2+ω+1=0.

objectives.label: Find repeated-root constants
objectives.description: Find the value of a constant that gives a cubic equation a repeated root, using the Factor Theorem and the two cases (shared root or discriminant D=0).

entries.text: An n-th degree equation always has n solutions when considered within the range of complex numbers (excluding cases with repeated solutions). $n$

A.why: General remark that an n-th degree equation has n complex solutions, not tied to one objective.

B.why: General remark that an n-th degree equation has n complex solutions, not tied to one objective.

entries.text: Heading of the method: how to solve cubic and quartic equations (step 1 Factorise, step 2 Find the solutions).

A.why: Heading of the method for solving cubic and quartic equations.

B.why: Heading of the method for solving cubic and quartic equations.

entries.text: Step 1 Factorise, quartic equations: if there are only x^4, x^2 and constant terms, treat x^2 as a chunk; otherwise use the Factor Theorem. $x^4, x^2$

A.why: Quartic factorising step: treat x^2 as a chunk or use the Factor Theorem.

B.why: Step 1 for quartics: treat x² as a chunk or use the Factor Theorem.

entries.text: Step 2 Find the solutions: the solutions of (x − α)(x − β)(x − γ) = 0 are x = α or β or γ. $(x-\alpha)(x-\beta)(x-\gamma)=0 \Rightarrow x=\alpha \text{ or } \beta \text{ or } \gamma$

A.why: Step 2 reads off solutions from the factorised form.

B.why: Step 2 of solving: read off solutions from the factorised form.

entries.text: Step 2: for (x − a)(ax^2 + bx + c) = 0, if ax^2 + bx + c cannot be factorised, use the Quadratic Formula; the solutions in this case are x = a or x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac))/(2a). $x=a \text{ or } \dfrac{-b\pm\sqrt{b^2-4ac}}{2a}$

A.why: Uses the Quadratic Formula when the quadratic factor cannot be factorised.

B.why: Uses the Quadratic Formula for the non-factorisable quadratic part when solving cubics.

entries.text: Illustration of a household water tank with pipes. Labels: COMPLEX INFLOW FLOW (LEFT) (top left), CONTROL VALVE (x = 1) (top right), STABLE LEVEL (water level inside tank), COMPLEX INFLOW FLOW (LEFT) (bottom left), REGULATED OUTFLOW FLOW (LEFT) (bottom right).

A.why: Water tank illustration only decorates the lesson.

B.why: Decorative water tank illustration for the lesson opening.

entries.text: A number that becomes 1 when cubed is called a cube root of unity.

A.why: Defines cube root of unity, the basis for working with ω.

B.why: Defines a cube root of unity, the basis for ω.

entries.text: One of the cube roots of unity that is a complex non-real number is denoted by $\omega$ (omega).

A.why: Introduces the notation ω for the non-real cube root of unity.

B.why: Introduces the notation ω for the non-real cube root of unity.

entries.text: $\omega$ has the property $\omega^3=1$. $\omega^3=1$

A.why: States ω^3=1, used to simplify expressions with ω.

B.why: States the property ω³=1.

entries.text: In calculations using $\omega$, first use $\omega^3=1$ to lower the degree of $\omega$. $\omega^3=1$

A.why: First lower the degree of ω using ω^3=1.

B.why: Uses ω³=1 to lower the power of ω first.

entries.text: After that, if $\omega^2$ and $\omega$ remain, use $\omega^2+\omega+1=0$ to find the value of the expression. $\omega^2+\omega+1=0$

A.why: Then use ω^2+ω+1=0 to evaluate the remaining expression.

B.why: Uses ω²+ω+1=0 to evaluate remaining ω terms.

entries.text: To find a value making a cubic equation have a repeated root, first use the factor theorem to factor the cubic into the form (x − a)(x² + bx + c). $(x-a)(x^2+bx+c)$

A.why: First step for finding the constant giving a repeated root: factor with the Factor Theorem.

B.why: First step for repeated-root constants: factor the cubic as (x − a)(x² + bx + c) by the factor theorem.

entries.text: Case 1: if x² + bx + c = 0 has x = a as a solution, substitute x = a into x² + bx + c = 0. $x^2+bx+c=0$

A.why: Case 1 of the repeated-root condition: substitute x=a into the quadratic.

B.why: Case 1 of the repeated-root condition: substitute x = a into the quadratic factor.
